subject: Reuse Arcscan's answer instead of spending its rate limit on every page load
body:

twenty-five minutes. The task page asked for its funder's history on every

activity section then reported the index as unavailable. Settlements are now
reused for thirty seconds, concurrent callers share one request, and a
refusal falls back to the last real answer if it is under ten minutes old.

subject: Tokenise the corpus on Hedera, and pay only runs a live human drove
body:

Asset Tokenization Studio factory on testnet (0.0.10520394, THNRC). Its control
list is a whitelist, so only an address with a World ID proof can hold a share.

dividends from sales are declared per share. The security is source-verified on

the binding before the proof is made, because the action allows one
verification per person. A verified human is added to the security's whitelist.

subject: Move Thenar to Arc, where the bounty and the gas are the same USDC
body:
This is the start of the ETHOnline 2026 continuity work. Everything before
commit e4f131d (3 September) existed before the event; the Avalanche build it
forks from is the history below.

AxonProtocolV2 is deployed to Arc testnet unchanged, and that is the argument
for the port rather than an omission. The protocol escrows and pays in the
chain's native value — msg.value in, a call with value out — and on Arc the
native value is USDC. A funder's bounty, an operator's payout and the gas to
submit a run now come out of one balance in one currency. On Avalanche an
operator needed AVAX before they could earn anything; here the thing they earn
is the thing they spend.

  AxonProtocolV2         0x6D6D6D0ee86C654b69646223049D6812c0218B2f
  PasskeyRegistry        0xecbbC9d43eF7C4E4Df00BC02757b8FC3E3b7615e
  TrajectoryCertificate  0x9dAc88a501F908FFaF41F4e0c6071c1F8B6B9B7B
  ContributionRecord     0x940a9A5CB219D5061748AD10b1Dd38f82C825523
  CorpusAccess           0x14588B2b26c3af1D0dDabc386fCe659d662B7Bc8

Five tasks seeded at five cents a run, 1.5 USDC in escrow, read back off the
chain after deploying. A fresh verifier signs for this deployment; the old one
lived on a signer service that no longer exists.

One unit to get right, and the comment in chain.ts says so where it matters:
native USDC on Arc has 18 decimals while its ERC-20 face reports 6 for the same
balance. Every amount in this app is native.

The content security policy names Arc's three measured RPC hosts, plus Blocky402
and the Hedera mirror node for the corpus paywall that is coming next.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: The referral pot has been paying since the beginning, from nowhere anyone could see
body:
Referrals is deployed, funded with five claims still in it, and has honoured
one. In this interface it was a row on the contract registry: nobody could see
whether they had been credited, nobody could get a link to give somebody, and
the newcomer who has to make the call had no way to make it.

The claim is the newcomer's, never the referrer's, and the contract is explicit
about why — a referrer who could claim on somebody else's behalf could name
themselves the introducer of every address that ever ran the station. So the
link is an invitation to a page carrying the referrer's address, and the button
appears on the newcomer's own wallet, once they have earned the 120.00 of
recorded score the contract wants before it will pay anyone.

Three states, all of them real on chain right now: 0x391a51f8 was brought by
0xDf93bd and cannot be claimed twice; 0xDf93bd has brought one of a permitted
ten; the pot holds five more. The claim simulates to exactly the revert those
facts predict.

subject: Name the new endpoints in the policy that refuses everything else
body:
Wiring in two fallback RPCs without adding them to connect-src meant the
browser refused every request to them. The whole page sweep went from 34 of 41
to nought, on the first run after the change — which is the content security
policy doing precisely its job, and the omission being mine.

They are named now, in the same order as RPC_ENDPOINTS so the two lists can be
read against each other, and a test asserts that every host in one appears in
the other. Two lists in two files that must agree is the shape of defect this
session has already fixed twice.

One retry per endpoint rather than three, while here. A public endpoint answers
a burst with 429, and retrying the thing that just refused is slower and
noisier than asking one of the other two.

subject: The bar that claims to know had stopped knowing
body:
Adding a second and third RPC broke the banner that reports on the first.
Conditions asked the chain's primary endpoint and nothing else, which was right
when the app read from that endpoint and nothing else. It would now announce
the chain unreachable while every figure on the page was being read
successfully from a secondary — and a false alarm on this bar is worse than no
bar, because it is the one element on the site whose whole job is to know.

It asks all three, and says the chain is unreachable only when none of them
answer.

Having asked, it may as well ask what time it is. Half the figures here are
times — a task's deadline, how long a sitting has run, whether a proposal's
voting has closed — and every one compares a chain timestamp against
Date.now(). If the machine's clock is wrong the interface reports the
disagreement as fact: a deadline shown as passed that has not, a run timed at
the wrong length. Blocks land every couple of seconds on this chain, so a
healthy skew is a few seconds and two minutes is a clock nobody set.

G5 runs the page on three machines — one correct, one 45 minutes fast, one 20
minutes slow — and asserts the banner appears for exactly the wrong ones,
naming the gap and pointing the right way.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: Ask more than one endpoint, and stop guessing what it will accept
body:
Every read on this site went to a single public RPC. If it rate-limited or went
down, the standings, the task list, the escrow figures and the contract
registry went with it — and since the API backend went away, the chain is the
only half of this product still answering.

Ten modules each built their own client with http() and no argument, so they
all failed together. They share one now, with three endpoints in order.

The endpoints are not equivalent, and shipping them as if they were would have
traded a dead endpoint for a live one that returns nothing. Measured before
being written down: the primary answers a million-block getLogs in one call,
publicnode refuses above about fifty thousand, drpc above about ten. This app
reads its own history in exactly those wide ranges.

So the range stopped being a guess. lib/scan-logs.ts asks for the whole span
and, if the endpoint refuses, halves it and asks for both halves — down to a
floor, past which a refusal is not about the width and is re-raised rather than
multiplied. Every log-reading path goes through it.

That is the third guess about this cap and the last one that matters. The first
was two thousand blocks walked back forty times, which expired and emptied the
standings. The second was a million in one call, which only the primary
answers. A range is a property of the deployment's history; the splitting is a
property of whoever is answering; and neither has to know about the other.

G4 proves it against the live chain: nine accepted runs found with the primary
up, nine with it pointed at a domain that does not resolve.

Four lint errors introduced earlier today are fixed with it — three synchronous
setStates inside effects, and the clock read during render that would have made
the server's date and the browser's disagree.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: Three ways the station meets a machine that cannot do what it assumes
body:
No GPU. A run abandoned halfway. A theme change that inverts every surface at
once. Each of them had an answer that was worse than saying nothing.

Without WebGL the viewport threw a react-three-fiber exception into the route's
error boundary, which tells a visitor something went wrong and nothing about
what they came to see. The support check runs on a throwaway canvas rather than
by sniffing the browser, because support is a property of the machine, the
driver and the user's own settings. When it fails the page names the task,
names the likely reasons, says there is nothing to retry, and points at the
parts of this product that never needed a GPU.

A run in progress was not saved anywhere. The draft store catches a measured
run, which is what made leaving after a measurement survivable; it does not
catch a run still being driven, whose samples live in a ref until the run ends.
Closing the tab took ninety seconds of somebody's work with it, silently. The
guard is on while running and released once measured, because from there the
draft has it and a guard that never lifts is one nobody reads.

And the ground crosses over on a theme change now, for the length of the press
and no longer. A standing transition on background-color would catch every
hover, every focus ring and every panel that changes tone under the pointer,
and make the whole interface feel like it is trailing the cursor.

qa-degraded.mjs covers all three. They need their own browser with its own
flags — switching WebGL off is a property of the process, not of the page —
which is why they are not in the page sweep.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: Say "we could not ask" when that is what happened
body:
A run page had one failure state and two failures behind it. "This deployment
has never stored that hash" and "the store did not answer" both landed the
reader on the same sentence — nothing on file for 0x363e…8485 — and one of
those is a fact about their run while the other is a fact about us.

It stopped being hypothetical this week. The backend this site rewrites /api/*
to is gone, so every read returns the platform's own 404, and every run page
told its reader with complete confidence that a run which is on chain, paid,
and recorded had never existed.

The status alone cannot separate them, which was the first attempt and was
wrong: a 404 is our route reporting no such hash and it is equally the edge in
front of us reporting no such application. The body can. Ours answer with
{ error: string } and nothing else; a platform envelope carries a correlation
id and a machine code. So "absent" is claimed only when our own store is the
thing that said so — and anything else says we cannot tell, and points at what
is still true, which is everything settled on chain.

Tested against the exact body thenar.io has been returning all week.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: The standings had gone empty, and the window that read them was the reason
body:
Every run on this deployment is now 207,760 blocks behind the head. useActivity
walked back forty windows of two thousand blocks — eighty thousand, which on
Fuji is under two days — so the leaderboard, the activity feed and everything
derived from them returned nothing. Not an error. A legitimate-looking empty
list, on the page whose whole job is to show who is ahead.

The walk existed on an assumption about the endpoint's range cap that is not
true: Fuji answers a million-block getLogs on this address in one round trip,
which is how the attestation and mean-score reads here already work. A range
anchored to the deployment cannot expire the way a window measured back from
the clock does. The standings come back with eight addresses.

Two more found while checking it was the only one.

The two engines had drifted. lib/server/sql.ts says the engine is chosen once
and nothing silently differs after that; `annotation` and `policy_submission`
were created in the Postgres branch and not the SQLite one, so /api/policy and
the annotation routes returned 500 against every SQLite database, new or old.
Nothing caught it because the tests and the deployment both ran Postgres.
A test now compares the two branches' tables in both directions.

And an empty corpus is a summary, not a missing resource. /api/dataset/summary
answered 404 for a task with no settled runs — a status this API's own OpenAPI
document does not describe, since it advertises 200 and 400 — which put a
console error on every page previewing a policy over such a task, and made the
"what the licence buys" panel vanish entirely. It answers with the same shape,
zeroed, and the panel says what is and is not there.

Three new features alongside them: earnings against gas on the operator page
(this address earned 1,247,525× what it paid to record the work), a nav
underline that travels rather than reappearing, and the tolerance drawn at the
size it actually is — on task 1 the spoon is 132 mm across and the band it must
land in is 25.

subject: Mark what was built, and write down the audit that found half of it
body:
Sixteen of the hundred are shipped and verified against the live deployment.
The order was not the ranking — building each one turned up the next.

Five of the sixteen were not on the list at all. They came from asking, late,
which write functions the deployed contracts have that no page can call. The
answer was eight; five mattered, and they are the ones a judge would have found
embarrassing: a 402 gate with nowhere to pay, escrow that could never come back,
a certificate nobody could mint, a record designed to be synced by strangers and
syncable by nobody, and a governance decision made and never carried out.

The completed test plan is regenerated alongside: 126 items pass, none fail, one
untested and named.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: A decision the contributors made, and nothing could carry out
body:
The Foundry is a treasury the people who filled the corpus decide how to spend.
It has a constituency it did not have to invent: every address the protocol has
paid carries a weight earned doing the work the treasury exists to buy more of,
and nobody can acquire a vote except by contributing. It governs one thing —
which task gets funded next — because a treasury that can only do one thing
cannot be voted into doing another.

It was deployed, funded with 0.01 AVAX, and reachable from no page. Proposal 0,
"Put the bowl on the rack", passed 165.00 to nil, closed on 3 September, and has
sat unexecuted since: a decision made by the people entitled to make it, and no
way to carry it out.

/foundry lists the proposals with their tally and their state, and offers each
action exactly where the contract would accept it — vote while the ballot is
open, execute once it has passed and closed. A vote button on a closed ballot
is an offer to send a transaction that reverts, and this page has enough real
state to be honest with.

Simulated before shipping: execute(0) returns task 6, so the treasury would
fund a real task on the hub; vote(0, true) reverts, because voting closed four
hours ago. Both are what the panel draws.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: The record that keeps itself honest could only be updated from a terminal
body:
ContributionRecord holds a non-transferable count of what an address has
earned, and it does not update itself: sync reads the protocol's own total and
mints the difference. The contract's own header says anyone may sync anyone,
and gives the reason — there is nothing to gain by syncing somebody else, and
requiring the holder would leave the record of people who never came back
permanently understated.

Nothing in this interface called it. So the mechanism designed to keep the
record honest for absent operators depended on somebody with a terminal, and
0x391a51f8… has been 189.00 points of recorded work behind its own token this
whole time.

It is on the operator page and the portfolio now, for any address rather than
only the connected one, for the same reason the contract takes an argument.
Simulated first: sync of that address would add 18,900, and sync of an
up-to-date one reverts — both branches the panel draws.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: Two contracts the product depends on and no page could call
body:
An audit of every write function against every page turned up eight the
interface cannot reach. Two of them matter now.

CorpusAccess.subscribe is the only way to buy what the corpus gate sells.
/api/dataset has answered 402 without an active subscription since the gate
shipped; the contract was deployed, verified, and read by that route — and
reachable from no page in this interface. A buyer met a payment-required with
nowhere to go. The product's entire revenue path ended in a status code.

/corpus now sells it, at the price and within the bounds the contract holds —
0.001 AVAX a day, 1 to 365 — read at load rather than written into the page,
with what it is and is not: it sells time, not rights, and every episode stays
readable one at a time by hash without paying at all. Extending adds to
whatever is left, which is what the contract does.

TrajectoryCertificate.mint had the same shape. The run page has shown "not
minted for this run" since the panel was written, with no way to mint it.
Anyone may pay the gas and the token goes to the address the protocol recorded
as the contributor, read from the protocol rather than taken from the caller —
so there is nothing to gate: the worst a stranger can do is give somebody else
their own certificate.

Both simulated against the live contracts before shipping. subscribe(7) from a
funded account returns an expiry seven days out; mint(1) returns 0xbad481be…,
the recorded contributor, not the caller; mint(0) reverts, because it is
already minted. Exactly the three claims the interface makes.

The shared write path takes an address and ABI now. It defaulted to the
protocol because that is where almost every write goes, and these two were
unreachable partly for that reason.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: The interface could not see that a task had ended
body:
lib/abi.ts was generated from AxonProtocol.sol — version one — and the live
contract is AxonProtocolV2. Everything the app called kept working, because the
app's list is a strict subset of the deployed one, so this was invisible.

What it cost was the two fields v2 added to a Task. A tuple decoded against
nine components reads the first nine correctly and drops the rest, so the
interface could not see `expiresAt` or `closed` at all. Task #5 has been closed
by its funder, has nothing left in it, and the hub offered a Run button on it —
an operator would have driven the task and been refused at the contract, after
the work. "Unfilled slots" counted its four unfillable slots too.

So the ABI is generated whole from the deployed contract now, by the same
script that generates the read ABIs, and the two fields are carried through.
A task that cannot pay says which of the four reasons applies — filled, minted,
expired, escrow returned — instead of "Filled" for all of them.

Then the funder's half, which is the bigger one. The protocol has two ways to
open work and they are not the same offer: createTask leaves expiresAt at zero
and a task that never expires can never be closed, so its escrow can only ever
leave as a payout. createTaskUntil sets a deadline, after which closeTask
returns what was never drawn. This form only ever called the first, so every
task posted through it was the unrecoverable kind, and the preflight I wrote
this morning said flatly "there is no refund path" — true of v1, which is not
what is deployed, and wrong on a page where somebody is about to commit money.

/post now offers a deadline and calls createTaskUntil when there is one. The
call simulates against the live contract and returns task 6, so the path is
checked without spending anything. The task page shows the deadline, what
happens to the money at it, and — only to the funder, only past it, only while
there is something to return — the button that returns it. Those are the
contract's own conditions; showing it anywhere else would be offering a call
that reverts.

Task #5 is the proof the whole path works: closed on chain, escrow zero.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: Show every write to the protocol, and name the ones we never call
body:
/contracts proved each contract exists and answers. It did not say what has
been done to them. Every transaction sent to the protocol is now listed from
Avalanche's own index — method, block, gas, fee, and the reverted ones, because
a log that shows only successes is the survivorship filter this project keeps
taking out of other surfaces.

Building it turned up that a third of that history read as "unrecognised
selector". The method map was built from AXON_ABI, which is the pruned list of
calls this interface makes, so anything resolving against it could name a call
the interface makes and nothing else. The three it could not name —
createTaskUntil, closeTask, submitTrajectoryFor — are real functions of the
deployed contract that the frontend simply never calls.

So the map is generated from the deployed contract's own compiler artifact,
forty-four selectors, by the same script that generates the read ABIs. It
cannot name a function the contract does not have and cannot miss one it does.
The operator page's call list gets the same correction for free.

It also settles what /post could only gesture at: the six tasks here were
posted with createTaskUntil, the deadline-carrying entry point, which is why
there is still no measured gas for the call that button makes. Named now
instead of described.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: Check declared difficulty against the ledger
body:
Difficulty is a number a funder types when they post a task. Every other claim
on this site is checked against the record, and this one never was.

It does not survive the check. Task #4 is declared easier than #0 and has paid
none of the two runs submitted to it, against three of three on the harder one.
Both tasks declared 3 have paid every run driven on them; two of the three
declared 2 have paid none. The bars are what somebody typed and the figure now
beside them is what happened.

Counts, not only a rate. Nought of two and nought of two hundred are the same
rate and are not the same statement, and at these sample sizes the count is
most of the information — the note says so itself rather than letting a
percentage carry more weight than two runs can. A task nobody has submitted a
run on reads "no runs yet" rather than 0%, because a rate over no attempts is
unknown, not zero.

The contradiction is found rather than asserted: the widest pair where a task
declared easier has in fact paid a smaller share, over tasks with attempts to
count. When the two orders agree the note does not appear, because a note that
fires either way says nothing.

Per run also gained a per minute beside it. Two tasks paying the same rate are
not the same offer when one takes 1:41 and the other 2:37, and par is the
task's own estimate of that — so the row now shows the rate an operator is
actually choosing between.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: Tell a rejected run what would have paid
body:
A run under the floor was told how far under, in score points. Points are not a
unit anybody drives in. An operator holds a joystick and puts a payload
somewhere; "4.90 short" does not tell them where to put it.

The score is a weighted sum of three terms they can each act on, so the same
arithmetic runs backwards. Solve for one term with the other two held exactly
where this run left them, and the answer is in the units of the thing they do:
come to rest within 22.8 mm of the seat, or finish inside 135 s.

Two cases have to be refused rather than answered. Smoothness is a quarter of
the score and cannot carry a 40% floor however perfect it is, so it is never
offered as a target — a target nobody can hit is worse than no target. And a
run that never reached the goal ring scores zero on every term by construction;
there is nothing to solve, and the taxonomy already says in words what happened.

The solver accounts for the penalty the run carried, which is why a run 33.40
short needs 7.1 mm rather than the 9.8 mm the weights alone would give. A test
feeds the named deviation back through the scoring and asserts it clears.

On the station under the points gap, and on the run page for any stored run
below the floor.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: Show the failure taxonomy where a person can read it
body:
lib/failure.ts has classified runs since the corpus started keeping failures —
a negative example is only worth training on if you know what it is an example
of. Its own header says the reason shown to the operator on the run page is the
same string shipped in the dataset. It shipped in the dataset. It was not on
the run page.

It is now, derived in the browser from the samples the page already has, so a
reader can rederive the label rather than take it. Shown on every run rather
than only the failures: on a run that placed inside the band the answer is that
placement was not the problem, which is a real answer, and a panel that appears
only with bad news reads as an accusation. Where the taxonomy knows the frame —
a payload let go in mid-air — the page will seek the replay to it.

Putting it there turned up something. Twenty-eight of thirty stored episodes
recompute to the deviation they were scored against. Two do not, both from
before "Measure the placement instead of being told it" — and one of them was
scored at 0.0 mm against a recording that ends 60 mm out, which is exactly the
claim that change removed.

Showing 4.3 mm in the header and 61.7 mm underneath without comment would be
worse than showing neither. So the disagreement is the statement: the run was
scored against one figure, the recording ends at another, and a gap that size
is not rounding — it means the number it was signed for did not come from this
recording. It is left as recorded. The payout happened, and restating it now
would be inventing a second history.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: Make the run driver measure the station, not its own precision
body:
Three things the first version got wrong, each visible only by running it.

It moved one axis at a time, longest first, which arrives along a staircase —
the worst possible path for a score that is a quarter mean jerk. It now drives
the diagonal with both keys down, and holds a long leg as one press instead of
four, because every gap between presses is a stop and a start.

It asserted "arrived" against a tolerance no control loop could reach. One
frame of movement is 0.42 × dt, about 7 mm, and the shortest press spans at
least one frame, so asking for four millimetres just spent sixty presses
oscillating. It reports the distance now, and the checks assert against the
tolerance that actually means something — the scorer's own 25 mm band.

And a keyboard-driven run lands anywhere between the high thirties and the low
eighties, so a single attempt sometimes missed the 40.00 floor and the panels
under test could not be reached. It takes up to three attempts through the
station's own Run again — which is exactly what this product tells an operator
whose run missed the floor to do — and reports how many it took rather than
hiding them.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: Tell a funder the two things the escrow figure does not
body:
/post priced the escrow to four decimals and stopped, which answers the
smallest of the three questions somebody about to commit money has. The other
two were on the chain the whole time.

The escrow is a ceiling, not a price. A run is paid the reward scaled by its
score, so only a run scoring 100.00 draws the full rate. This deployment's nine
accepted runs averaged 91.02, so ten filled slots at 0.004 draw about 0.0364 of
the 0.04 escrowed — its own record, not a worked example.

And what is not drawn stays in the contract. AxonProtocol has no refund path:
escrow enters through createTask and fundTask and leaves only as a payout, so a
task nobody finishes keeps its remainder for good, and so does every point of
scoring shortfall. That is the most consequential fact about posting a task
here and it was written down nowhere a funder would look.

The gas line is the interesting one, because it says nothing. Measuring it
turned up that the six tasks on this deployment were created with selector
0x5038a0a8 while the interface encodes 0xdb2399d0. Both are in the deployed
bytecode; the interface's simulates cleanly against the live contract and
returns task 6, so the button is sound — what does not exist is a real
transaction through it. The hook refuses to quote the other function's gas, and
the page says why instead of filling the gap with a number for a call nobody
made.

The cost hook is now shared. "What does this call cost" is the same question
for a funder posting a task as for an operator submitting a run, keyed by
selector so one path's gas is never quoted for another's.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: Say why the corpus is empty, not just that it is
body:
The empty list is the buyer's most consequential screen and it said the least:
four zeros and one sentence that fitted every possible reason.

There are three, and they are not the same answer to "should I come back".
Nobody has driven this task. Two people have and neither cleared the floor.
People drove it and never signed. Only the second and third mean the work
exists; only the first is a reason to go and do it yourself.

The distinction was one request away and was never made. When a filter comes
back empty the page now asks the same endpoint without the outcome filter and
counts what the task actually holds — 0 paid, 2 below the floor, 0 never sent —
then says which case this is, in those terms. An unworked task also names its
unfilled slots and its rate from the catalogue and links to the station,
because at that point the reader is the person who could fix it.

Two things the first draft got wrong and a real page made obvious. "Nobody has
driven on task #5 yet" is not a sentence. And an empty "paid" filter means
nothing cleared the floor — the copy said the opposite for a single recording.

A33 drives the chips rather than reading a URL, because that is how a buyer
gets there: task 5, which nobody has driven, and task 4, which two people drove
and neither cleared 40.00.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: Keep the sitting when the operator leaves the bench
body:
The station tallies the sitting because sessions here are long and repetitive.
It was thrown away the moment the operator left — which is exactly the moment
they want it. They leave the station to pick the next task, and the question on
the way out is how the last stretch went.

Nothing new is stored. The tally already survived the trip; it is in
sessionStorage, scoped to the tab. What was missing was somewhere for it to
appear, so it appears on the hub, with a link straight back to the task it was
worked on and a way to end it that only the operator can press. A tally that
cleared itself when somebody glanced at the hub would lose the thing it exists
to keep.

It also carries a best score now. A mean says how the sitting is going; a best
says what this operator managed on this bench today, and between runs the best
is the one they are chasing. Sittings started before the field existed default
it rather than being discarded — throwing away a tally to add a column to it
would be the worst possible trade.

R13–R15 drive a run, read the station's sitting, then leave for the hub and
assert the same figures arrived.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: Say whether running it again helped
body:
The contract caps a contributor at five runs on a task because repetition is
the point. PRODUCT.md describes the operator's real scene as long and
repetitive. The station's own copy, on a rejected run, says run it again.

And no surface anywhere said whether running it again had worked. Every one
showed runs as a flat list — a best, a mean, a row per attempt — leaving the
single number a repeat operator cares about, did this one beat the last one,
to be worked out by eye across a table sorted newest first.

So: group by task, order oldest first, difference. Only tasks driven more than
once come back, because one run is not a progression and a panel that showed it
as one would be padding. A decline is coloured and worded exactly as loudly as
a gain — the operator it matters to is the one it is happening to.

Two things the differencing had to get right, both now held by tests. The feed
returns newest first, and differencing in that order reports every improvement
as a decline. And "best" is the operator's best run on the task, not their best
so far — the first attempt is trivially the best so far, and a BEST label on it
tells the reader nothing, which is exactly what it did in the first draft.

Deviation and duration are optional on the way in. The two records this reads
are not the same record: the ledger keeps the measurement, the chain keeps the
score and the payout and has never held a millimetre. So the operator page,
reading the ledger, names what changed — 1.0 mm closer to the seat, 2 s slower
— and the portfolio, reading the chain, differences scores and claims nothing
it cannot see.

There is exactly one address on this deployment that has driven a task twice:
0x391a51f8… on task 1, 93.40 then 95.60. A31 asserts that page states up 2.20,
in that order, with the later run marked best. A32 asserts an address with one
run has no section at all.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: A two-object task could not be finished, and nobody had ever tried
body:
Driving a real run turned up a defect no page-reading test could see.

The station measures a run when the scene settles: nothing held, everything at
rest. A payload nobody has touched is at rest — it has been at rest the whole
time — so on a two-object bench the run ended seven hundred milliseconds after
the first object was let go, and scored the second where it started. "Put the
spoon and the mug into the crate" was unfinishable: 282 mm out, every time,
which is the mug's distance from its seat at spawn.

The rule the code beside it already claimed is the right one — a scene is
placed when all of it is — so the run now waits for every payload to have been
in the jaws at least once. One-object scenes are unchanged; they already
required their single payload to have been held. Ending early is still there
and still deliberate: that is the End run button. The same pass fixes at-rest
ignoring the second arm's grip, which only did not bite because a held payload
is usually off the table anyway.

With that fixed the same driven run scores 55–81 and is in tolerance, which is
what let the rest of this land.

What a submit costs, before signing it. The station said what a run pays and
never what it costs, and the two arrive together — one transaction records the
trajectory and pays for it. Gas only ever appeared on the receipt, after the
operator had committed to paying it.

It cannot be estimated the usual way: estimateContractGas needs the verifier's
signature over that exact trajectory, which does not exist until the submit is
under way. So the figure is what the last handful of real submits actually
burned, read off their receipts, priced at the gas the chain quotes now, and
split by which function was called — the passkey path verifies a P-256
signature first and is not the same transaction.

Measuring that turned up a second thing worth saying out loud. In all nine
submits on this contract the receipt's gasUsed is exactly max(what the call
needed, half the gas limit): one re-estimates at 394,668 and was charged
600,000, half of the 1,200,000 its wallet asked for. A wallet doubling an
estimate for safety is not buying headroom here, it is setting the price. The
panel says so. It is not fixed, because fixing it means pinning a gas limit,
and a limit pinned too tight fails a run for real.

And the number needed a unit. Fuji's base fee bottoms out at ten wei, so a
submit costs 0.096 nAVAX — fmtMon at three decimals renders that as 0.000,
which is a zero where there is a real cost, on a product whose argument is that
a measurement you cannot check is not a measurement.

qa-run.mjs drives it: begin, grasp, place, grasp, place, wait for the station's
own measurement, then read the panels. Closed-loop off the station's telemetry
rather than a fixed script of key presses, so it measures the station and not
frame timing — and on the platform's GPU rather than SwiftShader, because at
eight frames a second a keypress covers one frame or none.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: Carry the L1 proof and the Warp payload to somebody with a browser
body:
Two claims the project could make and nobody could check.

The L1 work — own gas token, fee schedule set at runtime, a policy delivered
to a second chain — existed as a script and a committed transcript. Real, and
unreadable without a terminal. /l1 renders it as three claims with the figures
that were read back off the chain, and says plainly that the chain is local and
you cannot reach it, because a page offering a button would be claiming a
capability this deployment does not have.

The transcript stays the artefact; a generator publishes it. The page first
read docs/l1-proof.txt at request time, which works locally and quietly does
not on the host: Next traces a route's files through its imports, and a path
assembled at runtime is invisible to that trace. Same failure shape as the
unanchored .vercelignore entry — builds fine, ships empty.

The licence receipt's Warp panel printed 320 bytes of hex and called it
evidence. Hex is not evidence: a reader who cannot read it has to take the
page's word for what it says. The payload is now decoded to its ten fields and
each checked against the same value read from the protocol by a different
route — nine of ten agree and the tenth is the protocol address itself, which
there is nothing on the page to check against. A disagreement would be the
finding and would be shown.

It also separates three things that were one thing. payloadFor is a view and
answers for any policy, signed or not. Attested is an event — a transaction
through the precompile — and policy 0's is real, at block 58,091,634. Delivery
is a third thing again, does not happen on Fuji, and is shown at /l1 where both
ends were ours.

A29 and A30 assert the figures, not the pixels: the mint, the fee floor, the
delivered policy, ten decoded rows with no crosses, and that each page still
says what it cannot do.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: Task 5.3: prove all three L1 claims on a real sovereign chain
body:
I had this down twice as out of scope, then as blocked on serving the L1's RPC.
Both were wrong, and the second was one flag away.

avalanche-cli 1.9.6 wants --use-local-machine together with
--num-bootstrap-validators 1. Those cannot be combined with
--bootstrap-endpoints, and --bootstrap-endpoints alone converts the subnet but
leaves nothing serving its RPC — a dead end, because blockchain join refuses
sovereign L1s and a node started with track-subnets in --node-config comes up
reporting no such chain. With the right invocation the CLI deploys ICM, starts
the relayer and prints the endpoint.

All three claims are then shown against the live chain, everything read back
rather than reported from what was sent:

  36  the chain issues its own gas token — 25 THN minted to an address holding
      nothing, the minter's own balance unchanged but for gas
  33  the operator sets what a run costs — base fee driven from 2,407,940 wei
      to the 1,000,000 floor at block 371, halving a 21,000-gas run
  32  a minted policy delivered to a second chain — minted on the source chain,
      announced over ICM, destination confirmed holding task 0, 2 trajectories,
      fee 0.5, ten seconds later

One thing the old README did not say: ewoq holds nothing on the new L1 and
claim 32 deploys its receiver there, so it needs THN minted through the native
minter first — the same facility claim 36 exercises. Output is committed at
docs/l1-proof.txt. The local network was destroyed afterwards.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: Phase 2: eth_call covers the accepting case too, so no wallet is needed
body:
I had 2.2 down as needing a funded operator key. It does not. A submission the
contract would accept returns the trajectory id from eth_call instead of
reverting, with nothing sent and nothing written — so the accepting case is
provable the same way the refusals already are. 2.1 existed only to unblock 2.2
and is dropped.

What it needs is a signature the verifier actually produced, and the verifier
only signs a run it has scored. C6.6 takes one through QA_SIGNED_RUN and asserts
it; without one it prints exactly what it wants rather than sitting dead.

It is deliberately not fabricated. /api/verify persists what it signs, and every
archived run predates payloadIds, which are part of the canonical hash — so a
signature cannot be reconstructed without inventing a run that never happened.
Putting a demonstration nobody performed into a corpus sold as human
teleoperation is worse than an untested assertion. Anyone who drives one
practice run can close it in a minute.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: Attempt the L1 for real, and correct the procedure it needed
body:
5.3 was recorded as infrastructure outside this repository. That was wrong: the
work was already scripted here — a genesis carrying chainId 88812 with the
native minter, fee manager and warp precompiles admin'd to the deployer, a
script that proves the three claims by reading them back off the chain, and the
matching deployer key.

So it was attempted. avalanche-cli 1.9.6 installed, a two-node local network up
and healthy, subnet and blockchain created with real fees, and ConvertSubnetToL1Tx
succeeded — the subnet is a sovereign L1. It stops at initValidatorManager, which
reaches the L1's own RPC on 9656 and is refused because the primary-network nodes
do not track the new subnet yet. Fixing that means editing avalanchego's config,
exposing a P2P port and restarting, which is system configuration rather than a
change here, and not something to do on a machine whose owner is asleep.

l1/README.md carries the corrected procedure. Its commands were written for an
older CLI and no longer complete: --bootstrap-endpoints is required or the
conversion fails with "conversion must include at least one validator", and the
private key must be bare hex or the CLI reports an invalid ending. Both cost a
cycle to discover and are now written down.

The local network was stopped afterwards.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: Final: one task unexecuted, and it is the one with no credential
body:
Every phase is worked through. Phase 2, which had been recorded as blocked
outright, is done apart from the accepting case: eth_call verifies the write
path's refusals against the deployed bytecode without a wallet, without gas and
without changing state. What remains is a signed run being accepted and paid,
which has to move AVAX and needs an operator key that does not exist here.

Verified against production with every runner exiting non-zero on failure:
23/23 pages, 10/10 deep, 37/37 API, 6/6 POST, 8/8 contracts, C1-C6.5 on chain,
57/57 route-mode combinations, 72/72 e2e, 57 unit, 108 contract, and a cold demo
rehearsal at 23.1s with zero console errors.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: Phase 2: verify the write path without spending, and finish 1.9
body:
A transaction is not the only way to ask a contract what it would do. eth_call
runs against the deployed bytecode at current state and returns the revert, so
every refusal the write path enforces can be checked for real — on the real
contract, with no wallet, no gas and no state change. Section C6 does that:
a settled hash reads as used, replaying it is refused, an unsigned score is
refused, an over-maximum score is refused, and the per-operator cap is read from
the contract rather than assumed. Only the accepting case is left, because a run
that is accepted has to actually move AVAX, and it says so rather than being
skipped in silence.

It also corrected me. I expected a replay to revert AlreadySubmitted and an
over-maximum score to revert ScoreTooHigh. Both revert BadSignature, because the
contract verifies the verifier's signature before it consults any business rule
— so a forged submission never reaches them. That ordering is the stronger
property and is what the checks now assert.

And 1.9 is finished: the soulbound certificate now appears on the run it
certifies, resolving the trajectory id out of the ledger rather than trusting an
off-chain index that could disagree with the chain.

subject: Task 1.9: the Warp attestation on the licence it attests
body:
LicenceReceipt is the most Avalanche-specific thing this project has built and
it lived only on the contract registry, which is a list. The place it means
something is beside the licence it is about, so the licence page now reads
payloadFor and shows the validator-signed payload, its source chain and its
length — or says plainly that a policy is not attested, which policy 1 is not.
payloadFor reverts for one that has never been attested, and that is reported
rather than dressed up.

The registry's recorded surface for LicenceReceipt is widened to match, under
its own rule that the surface is the honest answer and not the aspirational one.

ship.mjs now refuses a dirty tree. In a git repository the Vercel CLI uploads
what git knows about, so this component — untracked when the last ship ran — was
simply not in the build. It deployed clean and the panel was missing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: Phase 8: a demo that runs cold, and a rehearsal that times it
body:
docs/DEMO.md walks the five-step loop from a private window with no wallet and
nothing cached, each step ending on something the person watching can check
rather than on a claim. It carries the non-capabilities too, because saying them
out loud is better than being asked.

scripts/demo-rehearse.mjs runs and times the same path against production and
exits non-zero if anything logs an error: 22.8s across six steps, zero errors.
It found its own bug on the first run — step five took the first 64-hex string
out of the feed, which is a trajectory hash rather than a transaction, so the
one step that proves a stranger can verify the payout was silently reporting
'no receipt'. It reads tx_hash by name now and resolves a real one.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: Task 7.5: prove a snapshot restores, not just that it checksums
body:
The daily export has been running and integrity-checked for a while and nothing
had ever written one back. An export nobody has restored is a file with a
checksum, not a backup.

scripts/restore.mjs reads the newline-delimited snapshot, inserts every row and
verifies the result against the manifest the snapshot carries. Rehearsed: 18
trajectories out, 18 back, zero faults. Prop digests are checked against the
bytes rather than trusted from the row, and the target defaults to a scratch
path so a rehearsal cannot touch the live corpus by being run in the wrong
directory.

Together with the existing drill — which verifies every prop's sha256 against
its actual bytes on the real 22.8 MB snapshot — both halves of a restore are
now covered.

Also documented: submitTrajectoryFor is permissionless, so anyone may pay the
gas for someone else's run without being able to forge it. No relayer service
is running, and /contracts says that rather than implying the path is offered.
